title: The Faiss Library
relevance_reason: The paper is entirely dedicated to describing a core vector similarity search library (Faiss), its indexing methods, design trade-offs, and benchmarks, making vector databases and their core technology the main subject.
research_focus: The design principles, structure, and trade-offs of the Faiss library for approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS), including its vector compression and non-exhaustive search mechanisms, and its broad applicability across use cases.
method: The paper describes Faiss's architecture and design philosophy, explains the two main tools for managing trade-offs (vector compression and non-exhaustive search), benchmarks key features of the library, and discusses selected use cases to demonstrate applicability.
indexing_methods: quantization; non-exhaustive search; associative vector memories
application_domain: Trillion-scale indexing, text retrieval, data mining, content moderation, image search, recommendation, and multi-modal search
results_summary: The paper presents Faiss as a toolbox of indexing methods for vector similarity search, emphasizing that it offers a choice between a dozen index types and that the optimal choice depends on the problem's constraints. It explains the two core design tools—vector compression and non-exhaustive search—as the means to manage trade-offs in accuracy, speed, and memory. The paper benchmarks key features and highlights use cases in trillion-scale indexing, text retrieval, data mining, and content moderation. It also notes Faiss's widespread adoption, with 37k GitHub stars, over 5200 citations, 6M downloads, and reliance by major vector database companies such as Zilliz and Pinecone.
limitations: Faiss does not extract features; it only indexes embeddings produced by a different mechanism; Faiss is not a service; it provides functions run locally without concurrent write access, load balancing, sharding, transaction management, or query optimization; Faiss is not a database; its scope is intentionally limited to ANNS algorithmic implementation
research_gaps: Incorporating novel quantization techniques; Improving hardware support for some indexes; Developing new indexing forms such as associative vector memories for transformer architectures

title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search by Residual Vector Quantization
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a new vector indexing method (residual vector quantization) and search algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor search, which is the core technology underlying vector databases.
research_focus: Introducing residual vector quantization as an indexing method for approximate nearest neighbor search, particularly suited for unstructured vectors, and proposing efficient exhaustive and non-exhaustive search approaches based on it.
method: Database vectors are quantized using a residual vector quantizer into short codes of quantization indices. Euclidean distance is approximated via asymmetric distance (distance between query and the reproduction of the database vector). An exhaustive search method based on fast asymmetric distance computation and a non-exhaustive search method for large-scale search are proposed.
indexing_methods: residual vector quantization; product quantization; spectral hashing; KD-tree; hierarchical k-means (HKM); E2LSH; hamming embedding; miniBOF; small hashing code; small binary code
application_domain: Computer vision (keypoint matching, object retrieval, image classification, scene recognition)
results_summary: The paper proposes residual vector quantization for ANN search and two search approaches (exhaustive and non-exhaustive) built on it. Performance is evaluated on two structured and one unstructured dataset, comparing against spectral hashing and product quantization. The proposed approaches achieve the best trade-off between search quality, speed, and memory usage. On structured datasets, the method slightly outperforms product quantization, while on unstructured data it significantly outperforms it. The non-exhaustive search method is reported to significantly improve performance for large-scale search.

title: Manu
relevance_reason: The paper is entirely about designing, implementing, and evaluating a new vector database system (Manu), making vector databases the main and sole subject of the work.
research_focus: Design and implementation of Manu, a cloud-native vector database management system for billion-scale vector collections, with a focus on long-term evolvability, tunable consistency, fine-grained elasticity, and high performance by relaxing traditional DBMS constraints on transaction complexity and data consistency.
method: Manu follows a 'log as data' paradigm, structuring the system as log publish/subscribe microservices with WAL and binlog as backbone services. Write components act as log publishers while read-only search and analytic components are independent subscribers. Multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) and a delta consistency model simplify inter-component communication. Hardware-aware optimizations for CPUs, GPUs, and SSDs are applied, along with support for complex search semantics.
indexing_methods: vector quantization; inverted index; proximity graphs
application_domain: Recommendation, multimedia, language, medicine, security, drug discovery, e-commerce, video recommendation
results_summary: The paper presents Manu's architecture as a cloud-native vector database built around log-based publish/subscribe microservices, MVCC, and a delta consistency model to achieve fine-grained component decoupling. The system supports multiple indexing methods (vector quantization, inverted index, proximity graphs) with hardware-aware implementations for CPUs, GPUs, and SSDs. Manu was evaluated in three typical application scenarios to demonstrate its efficiency, elasticity, and scalability at billion-scale. The design relaxes complex transaction requirements in exchange for tunable consistency and per-component scalability, addressing feedback from over 1200 industry users collected over three years.
limitations: Manu is still far from perfect according to the authors; Current vector search index assumes a single type of storage (GPU memory, main memory, or disk); Existing vector search algorithms only explore some combinations of techniques for different components
research_gaps: Multi-way search: exploring how multiple search engines (vector, primary key, text) can interact and coordinate efficiently; Modularized algorithms: providing a unified framework for vector search allowing flexible combination of compression, indexing, and bucketing techniques; Hierarchical storage aware index: exploring indexes that jointly utilize all devices on the storage hierarchy; Advanced hardware: exploiting NVM, RDMA, NVLink, FPGA, and MLU for vector search and index building; Embedding generation toolbox: incorporating application-oriented toolbox with model fine-tuning and pre-trained models for rapid prototyping

title: Analysis of Adaptive Image Retrieval by Transition Kalman Filter Approach based on Intensity Parameter
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about image retrieval using Kalman filtering; a 'feature vector database' is mentioned only briefly in the abstract as a component of the retrieval pipeline, with no discussion of vector database technology, indexing, or nearest neighbor search.
research_focus: Improving content-based image retrieval accuracy and reliability using an adaptive state transition Kalman filter approach based on intensity parameters
method: Adaptive state transition Kalman filtering combined with feature extraction (edges, intensity, distance, angular motion) in a four-state space model, with similarity measures computed between processed image pixels
application_domain: Content-based image retrieval (CBIR)
results_summary: The paper proposes an adaptive state transition Kalman filtering framework for image retrieval that incorporates feature extraction for edges, intensity, distance, and angular motion. A four-state space model is used to estimate these features, and similarity measures are computed between processed images. The authors report achieving a 96.2% retrieval rate and state that they compare accuracy, reliability, and computation time against existing CBIR methods. The approach is presented as improving retrieval accuracy and reliability over prior content-based image retrieval systems.

title: A Novel Collaborative SRU Network With Dynamic Behaviour Aggregation, Reduced Communication Overhead and Explainable Features
relevance_reason: The paper is entirely about designing an intrusion detection system for IoMT healthcare networks and does not address vector databases, vector indexing, or similarity search in any capacity; the only reference to 'vector' is standard ML terminology for representing network features.
research_focus: Designing a hybrid multi-layer intrusion detection system (IDS) for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) healthcare networks that combines behaviour-based and anomaly-based detection with federated learning and interpretability.
method: A multi-layer architecture combining a Bloom filter-based behaviour detection module (layer 1) with an optimized SRU (Simple Recurrent Unit) anomaly detection layer (layer 2), trained via federated learning with dynamic parameter aggregation, and using LIME for interpretability of detection decisions.
application_domain: Cybersecurity and intrusion detection in IoMT-based smart healthcare networks
results_summary: The paper proposes a multi-layer IDS combining a Bloom filter-based behaviour module and an SRU-based anomaly detection layer for IoMT healthcare networks. The model achieved 99.27% accuracy, 99.28% precision, 98.73% recall, and 99.26% F1-score, outperforming LSTM, GRU, and other state-of-the-art approaches. The SRU model demonstrated superior handling of vanishing gradients with increasing network depth and faster training time compared to other RNN variants. LIME interpretability visualizations showed that feature F16 (related to IoMT/IoT device category) had the dominant impact on detection decisions. The federated learning approach with dynamic aggregation enabled real-time model updates across heterogeneous medical networks.
limitations: The proposed model needs to be tested with more data from different medical networks to verify its effectiveness and generality; The proposed model requires a large number of training data, which needs further research
research_gaps: Exploring asynchronous federated learning techniques to further optimize client-server communications; Testing the model with more diverse medical network data to assess generality; Reducing the large amount of training data required by the model

title: Vectorizing Database Column Scans with Complex Predicates
relevance_reason: The paper is about optimizing database column scans using SIMD vector instructions; the term 'vector' refers to SIMD processing, not vector databases or similarity search. It has no connection to vector indexing, nearest neighbor search, or vector database systems.
research_focus: Optimizing full table scans in column-store database systems (e.g. SAP HANA) by vectorizing the evaluation of complex predicates using SIMD instructions (Intel AVX2) on compressed column data.
method: A framework that categorizes scan predicates into range, vectorizable, and In-List types, and evaluates them using Intel AVX2 SIMD instructions tightly integrated with bit-stream unpacking of compressed column data (domain encoding + bit-compression).
results_summary: The paper presents a framework for vectorized evaluation of complex predicates in database column scans using Intel AVX2 instructions. It categorizes predicates into range, vectorizable, and In-List types and demonstrates how to bring predicate evaluation as close as possible to the compressed data format. Performance evaluation shows throughput of 6-8 billion codewords/s for most bit cases, with peak performance above 17 billion codewords/s for small bit cases. The AVX2 implementation achieves roughly 30% higher performance than the previous SIMD implementation, and in almost all cases scans need less than one CPU cycle per row, yielding over 8 billion rows per second on a single core.
research_gaps: Extending all algorithms to Intel AVX-512 with 512-bit registers; Utilizing mask registers to simplify bitvector processing and eliminate and/movmask instructions; Using cross-lane shuffles to replace individual lane loads with a single load and shuffle

title: Starling: An I/O-Efficient Disk-Resident Graph Index Framework for High-Dimensional Vector Similarity Search on Data Segment
relevance_reason: The paper is directly about the core technology of vector databases: it proposes a new disk-resident graph index framework for high-dimensional vector similarity search, compares it with existing indexing methods (DiskANN, SPANN, HNSW), and addresses a fundamental design challenge in vector database systems (segment-level indexing under resource constraints).
research_focus: High-dimensional vector similarity search (HVSS) on data segments in vector databases, where limited memory and disk space require a balance between accuracy, efficiency, and space cost. The paper proposes an I/O-efficient disk-resident graph index framework for this setting.
method: Starling, a disk-resident graph index framework with two components: (1) a data layout combining an in-memory navigation graph and a reordered disk-based graph with enhanced locality (block shuffling) to reduce search path length and disk bandwidth wastage; and (2) a block search strategy to minimize costly disk I/O operations during vector query execution.
mentioned_systems: Milvus; DiskANN; SPANN; ADBV; NSG; HNSW; Pregel; Ligra
indexing_methods: HNSW; NSG; IVFPQ; k-means; graph-based indexing; block shuffling; in-memory navigation graph; disk-based graph index
application_domain: Vector databases and data management, with broader applications in information retrieval, recommendation systems, scientific computing, and large language models
results_summary: The paper proposes Starling, a disk-resident graph index framework that optimizes data layout and search strategy for HVSS on data segments. On a segment with 2GB memory and 10GB disk capacity, Starling accommodates up to 33 million vectors in 128 dimensions, achieving over 0.9 average precision and top-10 recall with latency under 1 millisecond. Compared to state-of-the-art methods (DiskANN, SPANN), Starling exhibits 43.9× higher throughput with 98% lower query latency while maintaining the same level of accuracy. The block shuffling strategy achieves a 12× higher overlap ratio compared to a naive k-means-based assignment, demonstrating the importance of locality optimization for graph indexes on disk.
limitations: Starling primarily emphasizes query optimization for static indexes; data updates require an asynchronous merging process and comprehensive index reconstruction; The framework is designed for a single data segment scenario rather than a fully distributed system; The in-memory graph requires a balance between search performance and memory overhead, as a larger sample ratio increases memory usage
research_gaps: Apply Starling's methods to cache and GPU optimizations; Integrate Starling into Milvus for distributed optimization

title: The Term Vector Database: fast access to indexing terms for Web pages
relevance_reason: The paper describes a key-value database for storing pre-computed term vectors from the classic IR vector space model, with no involvement of vector indexing, similarity search, or nearest neighbor search. The 'vector' terminology refers to the Salton vector space model, not to embedding vectors or modern vector database technology.
research_focus: Building a database that provides fast access to pre-computed term vectors (from the vector space model of information retrieval) for hundreds of millions of web pages, mapping from page identifiers (URLs) to term vectors, and demonstrating two applications built on top of it.
method: The authors populated a database with term vectors for all pages in the AltaVista index, using compression techniques to reduce storage. The database's basic operation is a key-value lookup: given a URL, return the corresponding term vector. Two applications were built: an optimization of connectivity-based topic distillation and a web page classifier for annotating search engine results.
application_domain: Web information retrieval, page classification, topic distillation
results_summary: The paper describes the Term Vector Database, which maps page identifiers to pre-computed term vectors for all pages in the AltaVista index, enabling retrieval orders of magnitude faster than downloading pages via HTTP. Two applications are demonstrated: an optimization of connectivity-based topic distillation and a web page classifier for annotating search engine results. The database uses compression techniques primarily to eliminate redundancy within individual vectors. The authors report that the database enables a large class of applications that would be impractical without such pre-computed vector storage.
limitations: Current compression techniques work mostly by eliminating redundancy within individual vectors, making it unlikely to achieve another factor of two reduction by continuing that path; The database lacks content information beyond term vectors, requiring complementary services like the Connectivity Server
research_gaps: Looking for term candidates in more places such as alt text in tags and link text on incoming links; Supporting multi-word terms; Switching to a table-based stemmer to improve performance and support multiple languages; Exploring weights for terms influenced by markup (e.g., higher weightings for terms in titles); Exploring alternative lexicons; Improving compression by eliminating redundancy across vectors to cut storage requirements in half

title: QA-RAG: Exploring LLM Reliance on External Knowledge
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about RAG-based question-answering with LLMs; the vector database is only mentioned as the storage mechanism for the external knowledge base ('dense vector index database') without any discussion of its internals, indexing, or comparison with other systems.
research_focus: Evaluating a RAG-based question-answering system (QA-RAG) that relies solely on an external dense vector index database, examining its performance in noise robustness, knowledge gap detection, and external truth integration using Llama 2 models.
method: Proposes the QA-RAG architecture using Llama 2 7b and 13b with a dense vector index database as the external knowledge base. Systematically evaluates three RAG capabilities (noise robustness via varying top-k retrieval, knowledge gap detection, and external truth integration) on a modified TriviaQA dataset with ablation studies.
application_domain: Natural language processing / Question answering
results_summary: The QA-RAG approach with Llama 2 13b achieved the highest accuracy of 83.3% across all baselines on the modified TriviaQA dataset. The ablation study showed the dense retriever achieved 95% context recall, confirming its importance for system performance. Knowledge gap detection was better with Llama 2 13b (78%) than 7b (66%). However, the model still struggled significantly with external truth integration, where contradicting information in the knowledge base created tension with the model's prior knowledge. The authors conclude that considerable work remains to fully leverage RAG in question-answering tasks.
limitations: The model still struggles significantly in terms of external truth integration; Even if the retriever accurately provides necessary information, reliable answers are not guaranteed; The reliability of answers remains somewhat unpredictable despite effective retrieval
research_gaps: Developing retrievers capable of extracting relevant context with minimal noise; Resolving the tension between a model's prior knowledge and information presented in reference documents; Further work to fully leverage RAG in question-answering tasks

title: Emotion-Aware Embedding Fusion in Large Language Models (Flan-T5, Llama 2, DeepSeek-R1, and ChatGPT 4) for Intelligent Response Generation
relevance_reason: The FAISS vector database is mentioned only as a storage and retrieval component within the broader LLM-based psychotherapy pipeline; the paper's main subject is emotion-aware embedding fusion for LLM response generation, not vector database technology.
research_focus: Enhancing the emotional intelligence and contextual coherence of large language models (Flan-T5, Llama 2, DeepSeek-R1, ChatGPT 4) for AI-driven psychotherapy through a novel Emotion-Aware Embedding Fusion framework combining hierarchical fusion and attention mechanisms.
method: Therapy transcripts are segmented into word-, sentence-, and session-level representations using neural networks; hierarchical fusion with pooling techniques refines emotional representations; multi-head self-attention and cross-attention prioritize emotionally salient features; embeddings computed with BERT, GPT-3, and RoBERTa are stored in FAISS for similarity search and retrieval; retrieved segments are provided as context to LLMs for response generation.
mentioned_systems: FAISS; Flan-T5; Llama 2; DeepSeek-R1; ChatGPT 4; BERT; GPT-3; RoBERTa; Woebot; Wysa; Longformer; Recurrent Memory Transformers
application_domain: Psychotherapy and mental health support (AI-driven therapy chatbots, crisis intervention, hybrid AI-therapist collaboration)
results_summary: The Emotion-Aware Embedding Fusion framework was evaluated across multiple LLMs and practical use cases including AI-driven therapy chatbots. Experimental results show the framework enhances empathy, coherence, informativeness, and fluency in generated responses, surpassing baseline models. The approach outperforms standard RAG by integrating hierarchical embedding fusion and emotion-aware lexicon integration at multiple levels. The comparative analysis across Flan-T5, Llama 2, DeepSeek-R1, and ChatGPT 4 reveals whether newer architectures offer substantial or merely incremental gains in emotional understanding. The system demonstrates practical applicability in telehealth platforms and crisis intervention scenarios.
limitations: Token constraints restrict the model's ability to process long-form therapy sessions effectively; Challenges in ensuring coherence for long conversations; Adaptation to real-world implementation needs remains an open challenge; Standard RAG methods lack explicit emotional enrichment mechanisms (addressed but noted as a general limitation of the field)
research_gaps: Explore memory-optimized transformers (e.g., Longformer, Recurrent Memory Transformers) to retain extended session context; Investigate dynamic token compression and RAG to enhance response coherence in long conversations; Develop adaptive attention mechanisms to refine long-term emotional tracking across therapy sessions; Conduct pilot testing of AI-assisted chatbots with licensed psychologists and therapy institutions; Address ethical considerations and safety validations to align AI-generated responses with mental health guidelines; Fine-tune LLMs for psychiatric applications with more diverse datasets; Implement long-context models for handling extended therapy sessions; Conduct human evaluations to ensure the model aligns with therapeutic best practices

title: Chat2Data: An Interactive Data Analysis System with RAG, Vector Databases and LLMs
relevance_reason: Vector databases are used as a supporting tool within the Chat2Data system (for storing embeddings and caching queries) but are not the main subject; the paper does not propose, analyze, benchmark, or compare vector database technologies or indexing methods.
research_focus: An interactive data analysis system (Chat2Data) that enables natural language interaction with both structured and unstructured data, addressing three LLM limitations: hallucination due to lack of domain knowledge, high cost of LLM reasoning, and low accuracy for complex tasks.
method: A three-layer architecture: (1) RAG with domain knowledge paragraphs embedded and stored in vector databases to reduce hallucination, (2) vector databases used to cache frequent queries and reduce LLM interaction costs, (3) a pipeline agent that decomposes complex tasks into subtasks with multi-round reasoning to improve accuracy.
application_domain: Interactive data analysis: natural language to SQL for structured data, and retrieval/summarization for unstructured data
results_summary: The paper proposes Chat2Data, a prototype system combining RAG, vector databases, and LLMs for interactive natural language data analysis. The first layer embeds domain knowledge paragraphs into vector databases and retrieves relevant context to mitigate LLM hallucination. The second layer leverages vector databases to cache frequent queries, directly returning cached results to avoid costly LLM inference. The third layer uses a pipeline agent to decompose complex tasks into subtasks with multi-round reasoning. The system is demonstrated in two scenarios: unstructured data retrieval and summarization, and natural language-based structured data analysis with SQL generation and pandas visualization. An online demo is provided.
limitations: Existing LLMs suffer from hallucination due to lacking real-time domain-specific knowledge; LLM reasoning incurs high computational cost or expensive API usage; Existing LLMs have low accuracy for complicated tasks such as NL-to-SQL transformation; Traditional ML-based database optimization methods have high dependency on training data, poor generalization to schema/distribution changes, and low interpretability for multi-round dialogue

title: SeRF: Segment Graph for Range-Filtering Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a novel indexing data structure (segment graph / 2D segment graph) for approximate nearest neighbor search with range filtering, built on top of HNSW, which is core vector database technology. It directly proposes, analyzes, and benchmarks new vector indexing methods, making it central to a survey on vector databases.
research_focus: Efficient range-filtering approximate nearest neighbor search (RFANNS), where a query specifies both a vector and a range of attribute values, and the goal is to find ANN among vectors whose attributes fall in that range. The paper addresses the challenge that existing ANNS-first and range-first strategies degrade in performance depending on query range width, and that building separate indexes per range is quadratic in cost.
method: The paper proposes a 'segment graph' structure that losslessly compresses n HNSW indexes with the time and space of a single HNSW index for half-bounded range queries, reducing indexing cost by a factor of Ω(n). For general range queries, it proposes a '2D segment graph' with average-case index size O(n log n) that compresses n segment graphs, breaking the quadratic barrier. Optimizations are further applied to reduce index time and size.
indexing_methods: HNSW; NSG; DiskANN; segment graph; 2D segment graph
application_domain: General vector search with attribute filtering, with motivating examples in e-commerce product search, traffic vehicle re-identification, face recognition, and recommendation
results_summary: The paper proposes the segment graph and 2D segment graph as novel index structures for range-filtering ANNS. The segment graph losslessly compresses n HNSW indexes into a structure with the same time and space as a single HNSW index, reducing indexing cost by a factor of Ω(n) for half-bounded queries. The 2D segment graph extends this to general range queries with average-case index size O(n log n), breaking the quadratic barrier. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that the proposed structures significantly outperform existing ANNS-first and range-first methods for both small and large query ranges while maintaining a small index size and superior scalability.
limitations: The use of the structure for multi-attribute queries is still primitive; conjunctive queries can only choose one attribute for indexed search, leaving filtering on other attributes to online search.; The method is closely entangled with HNSW and is suitable only for static datasets and/or append-only insertions where the inserted point always has the largest attribute value.; Handling updates requires making deleted vectors dummy and rebuilding the index periodically, which is not efficient.
research_gaps: Building multi-dimensional indexes and developing query optimization techniques for multi-attribute RFANNS queries.; Applying the segment graph insights to alternative graph-based indexes such as NSG and DiskANN.; Coping with other types of updates beyond append-only insertions.; Developing more efficient update methods for the proposed index structures.

title: Color image retrieval using statistical model and radial basis function neural network
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about content-based image retrieval and feature extraction using autoregressive models; the 'feature vector database' is a simple storage mechanism for extracted descriptors, and no modern vector database systems, ANN indexing methods, or vector database technology are discussed.
research_focus: Developing an efficient content-based image retrieval (CBIR) system that extracts color, texture, and shape features using a Full Range Autoregressive Model (FRAR) with Bayesian approach, and categorizes them using a radial basis function neural network (RBFNN) with k-means clustering.
method: FRAR model with Bayesian approach for unified feature extraction (color autocorrelogram, improved EHD, micro-textures); RBFNN with k-means for image categorization; Manhattan distance of order one for similarity measurement; short-term learning relevance feedback for query refinement.
application_domain: Content-based image retrieval (color image search)
results_summary: The paper proposes a unified CBIR framework based on FRAR with Bayesian approach for feature extraction and RBFNN for categorization. The proposed improved EHD achieves a 44.14% retrieval rate versus 40.12% for MPEG-7's EHD, and the combined feature vector achieves an 84.97% average retrieval rate, outperforming MPEG-7 descriptor combinations (80.42%, 79.40%) and composite descriptors JCD (59.21%) and MSD (57.16%). The system demonstrates robustness against illumination changes, viewing angle changes, scaling, and rotation. The authors also show that the proposed technique has lower computational complexity than the compared MPEG-7-based and composite descriptor approaches.
limitations: The semantic gap between textual keywords and visual content remains a challenge in CBIR systems; Conventional micro-texture features have high computational and storage cost, necessitating their replacement; Retrieval accuracy of existing CBIR systems is still limited and unsatisfactory
research_gaps: The proposed work can be extended to incorporate other machine learning mechanisms for further improvement

title: Quicker ADC : Unlocking the Hidden Potential of Product Quantization With SIMD
relevance_reason: The paper directly proposes and evaluates a new distance computation method (Quicker ADC) for Product Quantization-based ANN search, testing it across multiple index types (IMI, IVF HNSW) within FAISS, making the core technology of vector databases—vector indexing and nearest neighbor search—its main subject.
research_focus: Improving the speed of Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC) in Product Quantization-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor search by leveraging AVX-512 SIMD instructions, generalizing the previous Quick ADC approach to support various quantizer configurations beyond 4-bit sub-quantizers.
method: Quicker ADC replaces memory accesses in ADC with SIMD shuffle instructions (AVX-512), introducing (i) irregular product quantizers combining sub-quantizers of different granularity (e.g., 6-bit and 4-bit) to handle 5, 6, and 7-bit shuffles, and (ii) split tables enabling lookup tables larger than register size. The method is implemented in FAISS and evaluated across multiple index types.
indexing_methods: Product Quantization (PQ); Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC); Inverted Multi-Indexes (IMI); IVF HNSW; HNSW; Inverted Index; polysemous codes; PQ Fast Scan; Quick ADC
application_domain: Multimedia retrieval, image similarity search, classification, and object recognition (evaluated on SIFT1000M and Deep1B datasets)
results_summary: The paper proposes Quicker ADC, a SIMD-based distance computation method that generalizes Quick ADC to support AVX-512 and irregular quantizer configurations. Experiments on SIFT1000M and Deep1B datasets with multiple index types (IMI, IVF HNSW) show Quicker ADC consistently outperforms polysemous codes and standard PQ implementations. For example, on SIFT1000M with 128-bit codes and a 0.25ms query budget, Quicker ADC achieves R@100 of 0.68 with IVF HNSW compared to 0.36 for polysemous codes. The ADC procedure can be up to 4× faster than reference implementations. The implementation is released as an open-source fork of FAISS for wider adoption.
research_gaps: Applying the shuffle-and-quantize principles to other quantization-based approaches that rely on lookup tables; Designing new filtering schemes where binary code filtering (e.g., polysemous codes) is replaced by lower-precision product quantizer filtering before full ADC computation; Exploiting upcoming processor improvements (Cannonlake 7-bit shuffles, Sunny Cove dual shuffle units) for further performance gains without algorithmic changes

title: DET-LSH: A Locality-Sensitive Hashing Scheme with Dynamic Encoding Tree for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a novel LSH-based indexing scheme and tree structure for approximate nearest neighbor search, which is the core technology underlying vector databases. It proposes, analyzes, and benchmarks a new vector indexing method in depth.
research_focus: Improving both indexing efficiency and query accuracy in LSH-based approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search in high-dimensional spaces, addressing the limitation that existing LSH methods focus on query strategies while neglecting indexing efficiency and suffer from performance degradation as dimensionality increases.
method: Proposes a novel encoding-based tree structure called Dynamic Encoding Tree (DE-Tree) that divides and encodes each dimension of the projected space independently, and a novel LSH scheme called DET-LSH that constructs multiple DE-Trees and uses a two-step query strategy combining coarse-grained range queries with fine-grained distance calculation, supported by a theoretical analysis of probabilistic accuracy guarantees.
indexing_methods: LSH; DE-Tree (Dynamic Encoding Tree); R*-Tree; PM-Tree; R-Tree; boundary constraint (BC) based methods; collision counting (C2) based methods; distance metric (DM) based methods
application_domain: General high-dimensional vector search / approximate nearest neighbor search applicable to databases, information retrieval, data mining, and machine learning
results_summary: The paper proposes DET-LSH, a novel LSH scheme built on the DE-Tree structure, to address the indexing efficiency bottleneck in existing LSH-based ANN methods. A theoretical analysis demonstrates that DET-LSH answers a c²-k-ANN query with a constant success probability. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that DET-LSH outperforms state-of-the-art LSH-based methods in both efficiency and accuracy. Specifically, DET-LSH achieves up to 6x speedup in indexing time and 2x speedup in query time over competitors while simultaneously delivering better query accuracy.

title: Vexless: A Serverless Vector Data Management System Using Cloud Functions
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is the design, implementation, and evaluation of Vexless, a vector database system optimized for cloud functions, making vector databases and their core technology (vector similarity search, indexing) the central focus.
research_focus: Building a high-performance and cost-efficient vector database using serverless cloud functions, addressing challenges of sharding, communication overhead, and cold-start times in the serverless paradigm.
method: Proposes three optimizations: (1) a global coordinator (orchestrator) that assigns workloads to cloud function instances based on available hardware resources for sharding, (2) stateful cloud functions to eliminate costly synchronization communications, and (3) a workload-aware cloud function lifetime management strategy to minimize cold-start overhead. Implemented using Azure Functions and evaluated against VM-based and naive cloud function baselines.
mentioned_systems: Vexless; AWS Lambda; Azure Functions; Google Cloud Functions; Starling; Lambada
application_domain: Vector similarity search in general; image search workflow is illustrated as an example application
results_summary: Vexless achieves up to 5.3x monthly cost savings compared to a statically provisioned VM-based solution and up to 6.5x savings compared to a naive cloud function implementation under sparse workloads. Under dense workloads, Vexless still maintains significantly lower monthly costs across all tested datasets. Search performance (recall) is comparable to or higher than the VM-based baseline across three different datasets. Tail latency analysis on the DEEP10M dataset shows Vexless consistently outperforms the VM-based benchmark across 50th, 95th, and 99th percentile latencies, demonstrating reliability and consistency.

title: SingleStore-V: An Integrated Vector Database System in SingleStore
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a vector database system (SingleStore-V): it proposes the system, details its core design and optimizations for vector indexing and search, and benchmarks it against other vector databases. Vector databases and their core technology are the central focus throughout.
research_focus: Design and implementation of SingleStore-V, a generalized vector database integrated into the SingleStore relational database, addressing the challenges of high performance and interoperability of vector search with SQL (filters, joins, fulltext search).
method: The system employs per-segment vector indexes, a vector index merger for scalability, a pluggable vector index architecture supporting multiple algorithms and libraries, auto vector indexing, and a Top() filter that enables pushdown of ORDER BY ... LIMIT to the table scan. Performance is evaluated on standard vector benchmarks against specialized and generalized vector databases.
mentioned_systems: SingleStore-V; SingleStore; Milvus; Pinecone; pgvector; AnalyticDB-V; PostgreSQL
application_domain: General-purpose relational database workloads combining vector similarity search with SQL analytics (OLAP and OLTP), including semantic search, RAG, recommendation systems, and image search
results_summary: The paper presents SingleStore-V as a full-fledged generalized vector database integrated into SingleStore, a distributed relational database. title: On Detecting and Removing Superficial Redundancy in Vector Databases

title: Enhancing LLM QoS Through Cloud-Edge Collaboration: A Diffusion-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach

research_focus: Optimizing the Quality of Service (QoS) of Large Language Model (LLM) requests in a cloud-edge collaborative setting by deploying vector databases on edge servers to cache QA results and using a diffusion-based multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm (DLRS) to schedule requests between edge and cloud.

results_summary: The DLRS algorithm with 10 denoising steps outperforms baseline algorithms (Greedy, MAPPO, G-MAPPO, T-MAPPO, LRS, DLRS-V10) in reward value, request completion satisfaction, and delay reduction. With at least 3 servers, the reward improvement reaches up to 22%. The algorithm also demonstrates scalability with more servers and adaptability to different training set sizes, though network structure adjustments are needed for larger datasets. research_gaps: Further improving the success rate of matching vector databases with requests; Addressing potential parallel inference issues in request scheduling; Implementing content-aware partitioning in the vector database structure to enhance query speed and reduce irrelevant results; Implementing a decision-checking mechanism to analyze relevance of prompt content provided to the LLM and reduce decision-making errors; Achieving load balancing by creating and allocating pods in Kubernetes for parallel inference

title: RoarGraph: A Projected Bipartite Graph for Efficient Cross-Modal Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is vector indexing and approximate nearest neighbor search: it proposes a novel graph index (RoarGraph) for ANNS, provides in-depth analysis of why existing indexes (HNSW, Vamana) fail on cross-modal workloads, and benchmarks the new index against state-of-the-art approaches. This is core vector database technology.
research_focus: Designing an efficient graph-based index for cross-modal approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) where query vectors are out-of-distribution (OOD) relative to the base data, and analyzing why existing ANNS indexes degrade in performance on such workloads.
method: Proposes RoarGraph, a projected bipartite graph index that uses query distribution to guide graph construction. The process involves building a bipartite graph between queries and base data, projecting it onto base data with neighborhood-aware projection to create pathways for spatially distant nodes, and applying a connectivity enhancement scheme. The paper also quantitatively analyzes OOD workload properties (spatial deviation, scattered nearest neighbors) to motivate the design.
indexing_methods: HNSW; Vamana; RobustVamana; RoarGraph; beam search (n-greedy search); partition-based approaches; quantization-based methods; hashing-based methods
application_domain: Cross-modal retrieval (text-to-image, text-to-video), recommendation systems, large-scale information retrieval, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
results_summary: The paper first quantitatively demonstrates that OOD cross-modal queries deviate 10–100× farther from base data than in-distribution queries, and that their k-nearest neighbors are spatially scattered, breaking assumptions of existing graph indexes. It then proposes RoarGraph, a projected bipartite graph index guided by query distribution. Extensive experiments on three cross-modal datasets (text, image, video) show RoarGraph achieves 1.84× to 3.56× faster search speed at recall@k ≥ 0.9 compared to state-of-the-art approaches. RoarGraph also reaches recall@k ≥ 0.99, a level unattainable by existing methods. A variant of the approach won the OOD track of the NeurIPS Practical Vector Search (Big ANN) Challenge 2023.

title: A novel system for strengthening security in large language models against hallucination and injection attacks with effective strategies

title: Tribase: A Vector Data Query Engine for Reliable and Lossless Pruning Compression using Triangle Inequalities
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is the core technology of vector databases: it proposes a new vector data query engine (Tribase) that improves cluster-based indexing granularity and introduces novel triangle-inequality-based pruning strategies for ANNS, directly addressing the central problem of efficient nearest neighbor search in vector databases.
research_focus: Improving the granularity of cluster-based indexes for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) and developing lossless pruning strategies using distance-based and angle-based triangle inequalities to reduce distance computation overhead in vector databases.

limitations: The curse of dimensionality makes vector distributions sparser in high-dimensional spaces, which affects the pruning effectiveness of triangle inequalities; Triangle inequalities introduce additional computational overhead that is further amplified when combined with hardware-accelerated distance calculations; Memory overhead of up to 1.76× the original index size is required for the fine-grained partitioning

title: Mitigating adversarial manipulation in LLMs: a prompt-based approach to counter Jailbreak attacks (Prompt-G)

research_focus: Mitigating jailbreak attacks (specifically Self Reminder attacks) in large language models by using a prompt-based filtering system (Prompt-G) that leverages vector databases and embeddings to detect and block harmful prompts in real time.

application_domain: LLM security and adversarial prompt detection in natural language processing
results_summary: The paper evaluated Prompt-G against four types of jailbreak attacks and found that 77.33% of 75 system prompts successfully induced fake news generation, while phishing, malicious content, and SQL injection success rates were 81.08%, 82.43%, and 74.32% respectively. When integrated with Llama 2 13B chat, the attack success rate was reduced to 2.08%, outperforming baseline methods including Vanilla SFT, Aligned SFT, Goal Prioritization, and Self Reminder. title: LLM-Driven, Self-Improving Framework for Security Test Automation: Leveraging Karate DSL for Augmented API Resilience

title: PDX: A Data Layout for Vector Similarity Search
relevance_reason: The paper is entirely about the core technology of vector databases: it proposes a new data layout, search framework, and pruning algorithm specifically designed to accelerate vector similarity search (exact and approximate nearest neighbor search), which is the fundamental operation underlying all vector databases.
research_focus: Proposing PDX, a vertical (dimension-by-dimension) data layout for vectors, along with the PDXearch search framework and the PDX-BOND pruning algorithm, to accelerate exact and approximate vector similarity search by enabling efficient dimension-pruning strategies.

Evaluated on 10 vector datasets across 4 CPU architectures (Zen4, Intel Sapphire Rapids, Zen3, Graviton4).
indexing_methods: HNSW; IVF; ADSampling; BSA; BOND; FNN; PDX-BOND
application_domain: Vector similarity search (exact and approximate nearest neighbor search) for information retrieval, LLM pipelines, multimedia retrieval, and code co-piloting
results_summary: PDX layout with auto-vectorized scalar code beats SIMD-optimized distance kernels on standard horizontal storage by an average of 40%. title: d-HNSW: A High-performance Vector Search Engine on Disaggregated Memory
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a vector search engine (d-HNSW) built on HNSW indexing, proposing novel system-level optimizations for vector similarity search on disaggregated memory, making vector databases and their core indexing technology the central focus.
research_focus: Designing a high-performance RDMA-based vector search engine (d-HNSW) optimized for disaggregated memory architectures, addressing challenges of running graph-based ANN search (HNSW) over a networked memory pool.
method: Hardware-algorithm co-design combining four techniques: (1) balanced clustering with a lightweight representative index to reduce network round-trips, (2) an RDMA-friendly graph layout preserving data contiguity under dynamic insertions, (3) query-aware data loading to eliminate redundant fetches in batch workloads, and (4) a pipelined execution model overlapping RDMA transfers with computation.
application_domain: General vector similarity search for AI applications including LLMs, RAG, recommendation systems, and semantic search
results_summary: The paper presents d-HNSW, the first RDMA-based vector search engine designed for disaggregated memory systems, addressing four challenges: pointer-chasing over the network, non-contiguous remote memory layout, redundant data transfers in batch workloads, and resource underutilization from sequential execution. Through balanced clustering, an RDMA-friendly graph layout, query-aware data loading, and a pipelined execution model, d-HNSW aligns HNSW search with RDMA fabric characteristics. Evaluation in a public cloud shows d-HNSW achieves up to <10^-2× query latency and >100× query throughput compared to other baselines while maintaining a high recall of 94%. These results validate the effectiveness of the co-designed approach for graph-based vector search in disaggregated architectures.

title: Contrastive learning and mixture of experts enables precise vector embeddings in biological databases
relevance_reason: The paper is primarily about improving text embedding quality for biomedical literature using MoE and contrastive learning; vector databases are only mentioned in passing as the downstream application context ('As vector databases become more prevalent for search and retrieval tasks'), with no discussion of database architecture, indexing, or system comparison.
research_focus: Improving the quality of vector embeddings for biomedical scientific text by combining contrastive learning with a Mixture of Experts (MoE) extension applied to pretrained BERT models, using co-citation networks as a similarity metric for training data construction.
method: A novel MoE extension pipeline where multi-layer perceptron sections of pretrained BERT models are copied into distinct experts, combined with contrastive learning (custom MNR variant) and special-token-based routing. Domain-specific datasets are assembled using co-citations as a similarity metric across multiple biomedical domains (skin cancer, COPD, CVD, parasitic diseases, autoimmune).
mentioned_systems: MPnet; E5; Mini; SciBERT; PubmedBERT; BioBERT; RoBERTa; ModernBERT; BERT; Llama-3.2-1B; TF-IDF
application_domain: Biomedical literature search and retrieval (scientific abstract classification based on co-citation similarity)
results_summary: The MoEall model (full MoE extension with contrastive learning) achieved the highest average F1max of 0.8875 across all biomedical domains. Single-expert (SE) models fine-tuned on individual domains generally outperformed multi-domain models for their respective domains, except in the autoimmune domain where MoEall narrowly won. The MoE extension increased average vector separation (vector ratio ~1.7 vs 1.5 for SEall), but the effect was smaller than in prior experiments with SciBERT, attributed to ModernBERT being a stronger base model. Notably, MoEall and SEall failed to outperform base sentence similarity models on CVD abstracts, and TF-IDF achieved the highest vector ratio but lower F1max, suggesting over-confidence in its representations.
limitations: MoEall and SEall failed to perform better than base sentence similarity models (MPnet, E5, Mini) on CVD abstracts; The MoE extension had less of an effect than in previous experiments using SciBERT, attributed to ModernBERT being a stronger base model; Popular pretrained models cannot distinguish differences in highly discriminative scientific literature despite further fine-tuning
research_gaps: Enhancing vector database search and compilation with the improved embeddings (mentioned as future promise); Addressing the limitation of prompting scenarios where self-attention across multiple documents prevents effective distinction

title: FedVSE: A Privacy-Preserving and Efficient Vector Search Engine for Federated Databases
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a vector search engine for federated databases, proposing a new system (FedVSE) with novel indexing, query processing, and privacy mechanisms specifically for vector database technology. Vector search and its core components (indexing, KNN/hybrid query processing) are the central focus throughout.
research_focus: Designing a privacy-preserving and efficient vector search engine (FedVSE) for federated databases that supports both KNN and hybrid queries while guaranteeing privacy across distributed vector databases.
method: FedVSE uses Intel SGX (TEE) for hardware-enabled security, a dual-indexing scheme combining built-in vector indexes with learned indexes for structured attributes, and an optimized query processing framework with indexing and pruning strategies to reduce communication overhead and query latency. The system is built on the Milvus vector database and deployed across six cloud servers.
indexing_methods: dual-indexing scheme (built-in vector indexes and learned indexes for structured attributes); indexing and pruning strategies
application_domain: Financial risk control, smart healthcare, intelligent transportation, and cross-platform trajectory similarity search
results_summary: The paper proposes FedVSE, the first federated vector search engine supporting both KNN and hybrid queries with privacy guarantees via Intel SGX. It is built on the Milvus vector database and deployed across six cloud servers. FedVSE delivers faster retrieval service than existing baselines (HE-based, SMC-based, and TEE-based approaches) in applications like cross-platform trajectory similarity search. The system addresses two key limitations of prior work: inefficiency for high-dimensional vectors and limited query support. The dual-indexing scheme and pruning strategies reduce both communication overhead and query latency.

title: AssetHub AI assistant: LLM-based querying for industrial assets
relevance_reason: Vector databases are mentioned only as a component of the RAG pipeline for context retrieval of unstructured AAS data; the paper's main subject is the LLM-based querying architecture for industrial assets, not the vector database technology itself.
research_focus: Design and evaluation of an LLM-based querying framework (AssetHub AI Assistant) for industrial asset data structured according to the Asset Administration Shell (AAS) standard, using a RAG architecture with a Semantic Query Mediation Layer (SQML) to bridge natural language queries and complex NoSQL data structures.
method: A multi-pass querying pipeline with a Semantic Query Mediation Layer (SQML) that acts as a semantic layer between the LLM and the NoSQL database. The RAG architecture combines vector databases for context retrieval of unstructured AAS data. Evaluation uses a benchmark of 120 questions across three difficulty levels, with comparative analysis against a baseline solution and McNemar statistical testing.
application_domain: Industrial asset management (Industry 4.0), digital engineering, querying of Asset Administration Shell (AAS) structured data
results_summary: The paper proposes the AssetHub AI Assistant, an end-to-end LLM-driven querying framework for AAS-based industrial asset data, and evaluates it against a baseline solution. The SQML architecture achieved 90.83% overall semantic correctness in retrieving requested information across 120 benchmark questions of varying difficulty. The McNemar statistical test confirmed that the improvements over the baseline are statistically significant. The SQML demonstrated the ability to handle complex nested, dynamic, and sparse NoSQL schemas without requiring model fine-tuning, while maintaining a model-agnostic mediation pattern. Qualitative analysis highlighted the SQML's role in mitigating structural and semantic errors in generated queries.
limitations: SQML depends heavily on the quality and homogeneity of underlying metadata (schema and data dictionary), which may be limited or unstructured in typical industrial applications; Generalizability across numerous large-scale industrial deployments of different domains has not been verified; Pipeline validated only with private LLMs (e.g., OpenAI models); performance with smaller open-source models in zero-shot settings remains untested; Multi-phase interpretative pipeline introduces extra delay compared to hardcoded database queries, posing challenges for real-time critical industrial orchestrations; Structural validity of generated queries does not necessarily translate to semantic validity in open environments with semantically ambiguous language, double negation, or schema mismatches; Graph RAG integration is a structural barrier for the recursive and nested document structure of the AAS standard, requiring complex ontological mappings
research_gaps: Automated and resilient ontological mapping to enable Graph RAG integration for hierarchical AAS data; Expansion of experimental setup to other industrial sectors and additional NoSQL database configurations to demonstrate scalability; Configuration of smaller (sparse and quantized) open-source, fine-tuned LLMs for near-real-time on-premise deployment; Introduction of context-adaptive re-ranking for a more resilient context retrieval scheme; Investigation of adversarial cases where structural validity does not translate to semantic validity; Testing the framework in heterogeneous multi-vendor industrial environments

title: SLAG: Scalable Language-Augmented Gaussian Splatting
relevance_reason: The vector database is mentioned only as a storage/retrieval component for embeddings ('we introduce a vector database for efficient embedding storage and retrieval'), with no discussion of its internals, index types, or comparison with other systems. The paper's main subject is the Gaussian splatting framework and language-augmented scene encoding.
research_focus: A scalable multi-GPU framework (SLAG) for embedding language-augmented semantic features into large 3D Gaussian splatting scenes, targeting time-sensitive robotics applications such as search-and-rescue, smart cities, and mining.
method: SLAG integrates 2D visual-language model features (SAM and CLIP) into 3D Gaussian splatting scenes. It eliminates the need for a loss function by deriving per-Gaussian language embeddings via a normalized weighted average of 3D Gaussian scene parameters, enabling highly parallelized encoding. A vector database is introduced for efficient embedding storage and retrieval, and a multi-GPU partitioning strategy handles scenes exceeding single-GPU memory.
application_domain: Semantic scene understanding, robotics (search-and-rescue, smart cities, mining), 3D scene representation
results_summary: The paper introduces SLAG, a multi-GPU framework that embeds language features into large Gaussian splatting scenes without requiring a loss function. By deriving embeddings from 3D Gaussian parameters via a normalized weighted average, the method achieves highly parallelized scene encoding. Experiments show an 18× speedup in embedding computation on a 16-GPU setup compared to OpenGaussian, while preserving embedding quality on the ScanNet and LERF datasets. The framework also handles scenes exceeding GPU memory through partitioning and iterative processing, and stores embeddings in a vector database for downstream retrieval on resource-constrained edge devices.
limitations: Existing approaches have limitations in speed, memory efficiency, and deployment flexibility; Scenes can exceed single-GPU memory limits, requiring partitioning and iterative processing

title: HAKES : Scalable Vector Database for Embedding Search Service
relevance_reason: The paper is entirely about vector databases: it proposes a new ANN index (HAKES-Index), a new distributed vector database system (HAKES), and benchmarks them against 12 existing indexes and 3 commercial vector databases, making vector databases the main subject.
research_focus: Building a scalable, distributed vector database (HAKES) that achieves high recall and high throughput under concurrent read-write workloads, using a novel two-stage partitioning-based ANN index with learned compression parameters and a disaggregated architecture.
method: Proposes HAKES-Index, a partitioning-based ANN index with a filter-and-refine two-stage design combining dimensionality reduction, 4-bit product quantization, and a lightweight self-supervised ML technique to optimize compression parameters. Decouples index parameters for search versus insertion to minimize read-write contention. Designs HAKES as a distributed vector database with a disaggregated architecture that separates the filter and refine stages across multiple nodes.
mentioned_systems: HAKES; FAISS; ScaNN; SPFresh; RoarGraph; OPQIVF-PQFS_RF
indexing_methods: IVF; PQ; OPQ; HNSW; LVQ; 4-bit PQ; dimensionality reduction; graph-based indexes; partitioning-based indexes
application_domain: Approximate nearest neighbor search over high-dimensional deep learning embedding vectors, with applications in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), search engines, recommendation systems, and multi-modal (text-to-image) search
results_summary: The paper proposes HAKES-Index and the HAKES distributed vector database, and evaluates them against 12 state-of-the-art ANN indexes and three commercial distributed vector databases on high-dimensional embedding datasets. HAKES-Index outperforms both partitioning-based and graph-based index baselines in the high recall region and under concurrent read-write workloads. HAKES achieves up to 16× higher throughput than the three baseline distributed vector databases at high recall. The aggressive compression (reducing dimensionality to 1/4 or 1/8 of original and using 4-bit PQ) combined with the refine stage yields superior throughput-recall tradeoffs. On low-dimensional datasets (SIFT 128d), HAKES-Index falls behind graph-based baselines like HNSW and LVQ, confirming its design is optimized for high-dimensional embedding vectors.
limitations: On low-dimensional datasets (e.g., SIFT 128d), HAKES-Index falls behind graph-based indexes such as HNSW and LVQ; Search throughput decreases after a large number of insertions and deletions due to additional vectors or tombstones to check during the filter stage; New vectors with distribution drift can impact recall for HAKES-Index; The index should be rebuilt when the dataset size changes significantly due to insertions and deletions; The learning technique provides little improvement for low-dimensional vectors not generated by neural networks
research_gaps: Handling out-of-distribution (ODD) queries where query and indexed vectors come from different modalities is identified as an emerging research problem in vector search

title: A Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation System with ReAct Agent Logic for Multi-Hop Reasoning
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a multimodal RAG system with ReAct agent logic; ChromaDB is used merely as a vector storage component without any in-depth analysis, comparison of vector database systems, or discussion of indexing/similarity search technology.
research_focus: Development, deployment, and empirical evaluation of a multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system based on ReAct agent logic, capable of multi-hop reasoning over textual, graphical, and tabular data.
method: The system uses ChromaDB for vector storage with separate collections for text, tables, and image captions; OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 for unified embeddings; GPT-4 for generation; and ReAct agent logic for multi-hop reasoning with automatic synonymic paraphrasing. Evaluation used a 50-query test set on the WHO Global Tuberculosis Report 2024, measuring answer accuracy, recall, and response latency.
mentioned_systems: ChromaDB; GPT-4; text-embedding-ada-002; CLIP; Active RAG; REPLUG; Toolformer; ChatGPT; Google Gemini
application_domain: Multimodal document retrieval and question answering over a medical/health report (WHO Tuberculosis Report 2024) containing text, tables, and figures
results_summary: The proposed multimodal RAG system achieved 92% answer accuracy, 89% answer recall, and 100% coverage of all data types (text, tables, graphics) with an average response time of approximately 5 seconds. Optimal parameters were empirically determined: k=6 for vector search, cosine classification threshold of 0.35, and up to three ReAct reasoning iterations. The system outperformed a text-only RAG baseline in both accuracy and recall while maintaining reasonable latency. The gap between textual query accuracy (94%) and graphical query accuracy (89%) was attributed to the limited context provided by lemmatized captions compared to full paragraphs.
limitations: The system represents images solely via their textual captions and cannot answer questions about colours or shapes; Limiting the ReAct cycle to three reasoning hops sets a practical limit on recall, as additional iterations yield only marginal improvements while noticeably increasing latency; Response times scale linearly with prompt length; The embedding model's linguistic nature reduces discriminative power for graphical content represented only by captions
research_gaps: Integration of pixel-level embeddings (e.g., CLIP) as a separate collection to capture visual semantics such as colours and shapes; Adoption of active learning mechanisms for document selection (similar to Active RAG) to reduce context size without sacrificing recall; Adaptively increasing the number of reasoning iterations for more complex queries beyond the fixed three-hop limit

title: P-HNSW: Crash-Consistent HNSW for Vector Databases on Persistent Memory
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is the core technology of vector databases: it proposes a new crash-consistent implementation of the HNSW index specifically for vector databases on persistent memory, including detailed design of logging and recovery mechanisms.
research_focus: Designing a crash-consistent HNSW index for vector databases on persistent memory, ensuring that the index remains in a logically consistent and recoverable state after unexpected system failures.
method: Proposes P-HNSW, a persistent HNSW implementation that introduces a lightweight logging mechanism with two logs (NLOG and NLISTLOG) leveraging the byte-addressability and persistence of persistent memory to guarantee crash consistency during insert operations and enable reliable recovery after system crashes.
mentioned_systems: P-HNSW; Annoy; DiskANN; HNSW; NVDIMM-N; CXL-SSD; CMM-H
indexing_methods: HNSW; LSH; DiskANN; Annoy; k-NN; ANNS
application_domain: Vector databases and approximate nearest neighbor search on persistent memory hardware
results_summary: The paper designs P-HNSW, a crash-consistent HNSW on persistent memory, using a two-log mechanism (NLOG and NLISTLOG) to handle insert operations and recovery. The authors provide a detailed analysis of failure scenarios showing how the logging ensures consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the logging overhead is negligible compared to the benefits of persistence. P-HNSW outperforms SSD-based recovery mechanisms in terms of performance while guaranteeing robustness and persistence for vector indexes.
limitations: The approach focuses exclusively on HNSW; applicability to other ANN indexes such as DiskANN or Annoy remains an open question.; Evaluation was conducted on x86-based platforms with emulated persistent memory, so behavior on ARM-based processors or eADR-enabled systems may differ.
research_gaps: Extending crash consistency techniques to a broader range of ANN indexes beyond HNSW.; Evaluating P-HNSW on diverse persistent memory hardware platforms such as ARM-based processors and eADR-enabled systems.

title: Interacting with vector databases by means of domain-specific language
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a domain-specific language and MDSD approach for accessing vector databases, not vector database technology itself (indexing, similarity search). Vector databases are the application domain and their interfaces are compared in depth, but the core contribution is the software engineering solution (vecDSL), making vector databases a substantial but not primary subject.
research_focus: Proposing a model-driven software development (MDSD) solution centered on a domain-specific language (vecDSL) to provide uniform, vendor-agnostic access to diverse vector database management systems, addressing issues of tight coupling, interoperability, and usability.
method: Design and evaluation of vecDSL, a declarative prototype language, within an MDSD framework. The evaluation compares the syntactic and structural properties of vecDSL (token counts, nesting depth, Halstead Volume, keyword counts) against the query languages of multiple vector database systems.
mentioned_systems: Milvus; OpenSearch; Apache Cassandra; Chroma; Weaviate; Qdrant; Pinecone; DeepLake; SvectorDB; Microsoft Azure AI Search; Elasticsearch; SQLAlchemy; TypeORM
application_domain: Vector database access and software engineering for uniform database interaction
results_summary: The paper designs vecDSL as a declarative language to abstract vendor-specific vector database APIs and evaluates its syntactic properties against existing query languages. The evaluation shows vecDSL achieves lower token counts (301), zero nesting depth, no function calls, and a Halstead Volume of 1681.45, indicating lower syntactic complexity than SQL-inspired or JSON-based interfaces. The authors conclude vecDSL effectively simplifies basic vector database interactions and provides portability across systems, but its limited expressiveness (no nesting, no functions) restricts advanced query scenarios. The paper identifies the need for controlled nesting, basic function support, and integration into mainstream programming environments as necessary refinements.
limitations: The number of keywords in vecDSL is notably high, increasing cognitive load; Absence of nesting structures and function calls limits expressiveness and flexibility for complex queries; The initial evaluation focused solely on syntax without user-based studies; No quantitative performance benchmarks (script generation latency, scheduler overhead, end-to-end query throughput) were conducted; vecDSL was developed for a dedicated code editor rather than being integrated into existing programming environments
research_gaps: Conducting a user-based study using a structured framework such as FQAD to assess vecDSL with academic researchers and industry developers; Establishing comprehensive performance benchmarks measuring script generation latency, scheduler overhead, and end-to-end query throughput against native APIs; Integrating vecDSL as a built-in module or library within mainstream programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Go); Introducing controlled nesting and basic function support to enhance expressiveness while preserving minimalism; Reducing keyword usage by consolidating semantically similar terms or introducing contextual keyword behavior; Conducting empirical evaluation of integration modalities (language-specific module vs. language-agnostic API)

title: Turbocharging Vector Databases Using Modern SSDs
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is the core technology of vector databases: it proposes, implements, and evaluates I/O optimizations specifically for disk-based HNSW ANN indices, making vector database indexing and search the central topic.
research_focus: Optimizing I/O performance of disk-based vector databases that use graph-based ANN indices (HNSW) by exploiting modern SSD parallelism, improving cache hit ratios, and reducing random disk accesses.
method: Three optimization strategies are proposed and implemented in pgvector: (1) parallel I/O via io_uring to exploit SSD concurrency, (2) spatially-aware insertion reordering to group similar insertions and improve locality, and (3) locality-preserving colocation to restructure index layouts and minimize random disk accesses. Extensive evaluations are conducted on real-world datasets.
application_domain: Large-scale semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for AI/LLM applications
results_summary: The paper addresses I/O bottlenecks in disk-based HNSW vector databases by introducing three SSD-aware optimizations implemented within pgvector. The combined optimizations yield up to 11.1× improvement in query throughput, a 3.23× increase in cache hit ratio, and a 98.4% reduction in index build time. Each technique independently achieves substantial gains, with the combined application producing the largest improvements. The results demonstrate that with proper I/O optimizations, disk-based dynamic vector databases can approach the query performance of highly optimized static indices like DiskANN while supporting continuous updates.
research_gaps: Further refining SSD-aware indexing mechanisms; Extending the proposed optimizations to other vector database frameworks beyond pgvector

title: Vector Storage Based Long-term Memory Research on LLM

research_focus: Proposing a vector-storage-based long-term memory mechanism (VIMBank) for LLM-based intelligent agents to improve decision quality and reasoning efficiency in complex multi-task scenarios by storing, retrieving, and dynamically updating historical interaction data.
method: VIMBank uses a vector database as the underlying storage layer for vectorized historical interaction data (knowledge, dialog, task information), combined with a dynamic memory updating strategy based on the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve to selectively forget unimportant memories and reinforce critical ones. Different retrieval strategies are designed for different types of interaction information. The mechanism is evaluated on ALFWorld, HotpotQA, and KAgentBench datasets using open-source models (Qwen2-7b, chatglm3-6b) and closed-source models (ChatGPT).

application_domain: LLM-based intelligent agent decision-making, multi-task planning, and long-term dialogue systems
results_summary: The paper proposes VIMBank, a long-term memory mechanism that stores vectorized historical interaction data in a vector database and applies an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve-based dynamic updating strategy. Experiments on ALFWorld, HotpotQA, and KAgentBench show that VIMBank increases the task decision success rate by 10% to 20% compared to different agent baselines. The reasoning cost is reduced by approximately 23%. The mechanism is demonstrated to be versatile, adapting to both open-source models (Qwen2-7b, chatglm3-6b) and closed-source models (ChatGPT). title: Not Small Enough? SegPQ: A Learned Approach to Compress Product Quantization Codebooks
relevance_reason: The paper's main subject is a novel compression method for Product Quantization codebooks, which is a core indexing technology underlying vector databases and ANN search. It directly proposes, analyzes, and benchmarks improvements to a fundamental component of vector database systems.
research_focus: Lossless compression of Product Quantization (PQ) codebooks to reduce memory footprint of vector databases, enabling deployment of ANN-based retrieval on resource-constrained edge devices.
method: SegPQ compresses PQ codebooks by (1) projecting codewords to integer sorting keys via binary concatenation (BinCat), (2) reordering the codebook to fit an optimal Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA) model under an error constraint ε, and (3) storing the residuals between PLA predictions and true codewords together with the line segments as the compressed codebook. Theoretical analysis establishes coverage bounds for the ε-PLA model without relying on the gap model used by PGM-Index.
indexing_methods: Product Quantization (PQ); Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH); Proximity Graph; Vector Quantization; k-means clustering
application_domain: LLM-enhanced applications (RAG, open-domain question answering) on resource-constrained edge devices; web-scale vector search
results_summary: SegPQ robustly achieves the highest compression ratio among all baselines and is the only method that keeps memory below 1 GiB for 1 billion vectors. Construction overhead is negligible (less than 3.4% of PQ training time), and query overhead is under 6% of overall ANN query processing. Compared to the state-of-the-art DeltaPQ, SegPQ demonstrates superiority in memory footprint, construction efficiency, and query efficiency simultaneously. Theoretical results confirm that SegPQ maintains comparable asymptotic performance even under non-uniform codebook distributions.
limitations: BinCat projection generates excessively large value spaces for high-bit-width codebooks (e.g., PQ128/PQ256), impairing learned PLA efficacy; Codeword reordering inevitably modifies original vector ID assignments, requiring a generic scenario assumption that IDs can be safely updated; For high-bit-width codebooks, only partial compression (upper 64 bits) is supported, yielding lower compression ratios (1.43× for PQ128, 1.18× for PQ256)
research_gaps: Embedding SegPQ into prevalent VectorDB engines to facilitate seamless integration of vector search on edge devices; Further theoretical analysis of SegPQ under non-uniform codebook distributions (generalized bound provided but full treatment deferred to technical report)
